column3: Near-verbatim parallel: lasting righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and final return.
The immediately preceding parable portrays worldly life as vegetation that quickly becomes scattered debris.
God is named better and more enduring, reinforcing the focus's measure of lasting value.
Contrasts the temporary enjoyment of worldly gifts with what is better and more enduring with God.
The immediate continuation moves from worldly evaluation to the Day when all are gathered.
States the same governing comparison: the Hereafter is better and more enduring.
Explicitly calls worldly goods and adornment temporary, while what is with God is better and enduring.
Its immediate resurrection scene strips away worldly distinctions before the Lord.
The destruction that leaves none remaining is only an indirect contrast to enduring righteous remains.
The local conclusion identifies God's reward and outcome as better than worldly security.
The next local accounting scene shows every deed present and counted before God.
Fair dealing is righteous conduct, but the verse does not develop the focus's temporal value contrast.
Directs seekers of worldly reward to God, who holds both worldly and afterlife recompense.
The warning against taking Iblis and his offspring as allies does not clarify adornment or lasting deeds.
The better outcome of returning disputes to divine authority is not a close parallel to the focus.
Directly prohibits extending one's gaze toward worldly splendor and calls the Lord's provision better and enduring.
Its rejection of misguided helpers concerns creation-witness and does not illuminate the focus.
Leaving outstanding usury does not materially develop the contrast between adornment and lasting good deeds.
Qualifies the focus by affirming that God's adornment and good provision are not themselves forbidden.
The failure of alleged partners to answer is unrelated to the focus's valuation of wealth and children.
God-given capability is better than tribute, but the construction narrative is only distantly related.
The rhetorical contrast over sons does not develop wealth, transience, or righteous deeds.
The local vision of unavoidable Fire supplies the consequential horizon for misplaced worldly valuation.
A sacred remnant from prophetic households concerns inherited signs, not enduring righteous action.
Near-verbatim local parallel: do not seek the adornment of worldly life over devoted remembrance.
Human contentiousness does not clarify the focus's contrast of values.
Offers what is better than desired worldly things: enduring gardens and divine approval for the mindful.
Condemns excessive love of wealth, directly challenging its treatment as ultimate value.
The nearby refusal of guidance supplies only a broad backdrop for worldly misvaluation.
Calling prophets among the excellent does not address worldly adornment or abiding reward.
All that passes away is set against the enduring Face of the Lord.
Rejecting revealed signs through argument does not closely develop the focus's value comparison.
Reframes wealth and selves as resources for faithful striving, rather than as worldly adornment.
Promises that no righteous work is lost and names God's reward as the best recompense.
Forgetting what one's hands sent ahead links rejection of guidance to the lasting significance of deeds.
A better replacement is defined by purity and mercy rather than visible possession, including a child relation.
Explicitly names Pharaoh's worldly adornment and wealth as instruments of diversion from God's way.
The local delay of punishment and fixed appointment only indirectly supports the focus's ultimate horizon.
The appeal to the best of merciful does not concern temporary adornment or enduring deeds.
Faith and righteous deeds are joined to the gardens of lasting bliss.
The destruction of unjust towns offers a broad consequence but not the focus's central comparison.
Affirms that even the smallest good deed will be seen, supporting the lasting weight of righteous action.
Direct local parallel: earthly things are adornment and a test of who does best in deeds.
Chosen excellence is not a close neighbour to the focus's contrast between worldly and lasting value.
Identifies believers who do righteous deeds as the best of creation.
The prophet's receptive mercy is unrelated to wealth, children, or enduring deeds.
Defines true righteousness through faith, giving wealth, worship, and steadfastness rather than outward display.
God's reward is better for believers who do good, explicitly correcting attraction to Qarun's wealth.
The people's ornaments become material for deviation in the calf episode, warning against adornment's pull.
The nearby garden warning exposes the fragility of material abundance and anticipates something better from God.
Faith, righteous deeds, prayer, and charity receive their reward with the Lord.
Questions the assumption that rapid worldly provision is simply a sign of good.
Faith and righteous deeds lead to inclusion among the righteous, though without the temporal contrast.
Withholding good describes corrupt conduct but does not address temporary adornment or lasting reward.
Wealth and sons are shown as the status behind an arrogant rejection, echoing the focus's named adornments.
The benefit of believing the messenger is too general to clarify the focus's valuation contrast.
God's recompense is better for those who believe and are mindful.
Good deeds receive a better return, supporting the focus's claim that righteous action has superior reward.
Rejects abundance of wealth as the measure of rightful leadership.
The superiority of God over partners does not develop worldly adornment or abiding righteous deeds.
Following guidance is a broad positive parallel without the focus's contrast of values.
The survival of Noah's descendants supplies a limited contrast between biological continuation and lasting good.
Temporary eating, enjoyment, and distracting hope are condemned as a short-sighted orientation.
Patience in a procedural setting does not clarify the focus's contrast.
A conditional pledge under plague is unrelated to wealth, adornment, or enduring deeds.
A believing group's prayer is devotional but only distantly related to the focus.
Explicitly lists sons and accumulated wealth as beloved worldly enjoyment, then directs to God's better return.
Hoarding good describes a related disposition but not the focus's temporal comparison.
Distinguishes worldly reward from the excellent reward of the Hereafter for those who do good.
God as the best guardian is unrelated to temporary adornment and righteous remains.
Worldly luxury is declared temporary enjoyment, while the Hereafter with the Lord belongs to the mindful.
Love of prized goods becomes blameworthy when it distracts from remembering the Lord.
Rejoicing in worldly life is corrected by calling it only a brief provision beside the Hereafter.
The Hereafter's abode is better for the mindful, joined to doing good in this life.
Pairs goodness in this world with Abraham's standing among the righteous in the Hereafter.
Its image of leaving nothing remaining offers an indirect negative contrast to deeds that endure.
Near-exact parallel: worldly life is adornment and competition in wealth and children, then fades away.
A prayer for a blessed landing does not bear on worldly adornment or enduring righteous deeds.
Worldly life is play and diversion, whereas the Hereafter is better for the mindful.
The more enduring punishment of the Hereafter gives a consequence, but not the focus's positive deed contrast.
Directly names the error of preferring worldly life.
The drowning of those left behind does not clarify the focus's meaning.
Directly identifies choosing worldly life as the misplaced preference at issue.
Racing toward good is a general action parallel without the focus's enduring-value contrast.
Worldly life is made attractive to disbelievers, while the mindful are raised above them on the Day of Resurrection.
The question whether any remnant remains indirectly contrasts extinction with what truly abides.
Worldly life is deceptive enjoyment, while full wages are paid on the Day of Resurrection.
The inherited Book is carried through graded commitment, culminating in those foremost in good deeds.
Directly contrasts desiring worldly life and its adornment with a higher prophetic commitment.
A lasting word among descendants is a limited analogy to an enduring legacy, not righteous deeds themselves.
A location at the lote tree does not relate to the focus's themes.
Its warning about manipulation of judgment does not clarify wealth, children, or lasting actions.
Migration, striving, and patience are righteous but the verse lacks the focus's value contrast.
Universal divine witnessing and the written record support the enduring accountability of every deed.
Household eating permissions do not bear on the focus's central comparison.
The challenge about rejecting revelation does not illuminate worldly adornment or abiding deeds.
God as the source of wealth qualifies human possession but does not develop the full contrast.
The description of punishment's environment has no meaningful relation to the focus.
Remembering it by choice does not develop wealth, adornment, or righteous remains.
The brief warning that they will know offers no specific neighbour relation.
Explicitly condemns exchanging the Hereafter for worldly life, the reversal corrected by the focus.
Those who seek only worldly good are contrasted with the wider horizon of the Hereafter.
The prayer for good in this world and the Hereafter qualifies the focus's value hierarchy without denying worldly good.
Distinguishes the reward sought in this world from the reward sought in the Hereafter.
Commands believers to trade worldly life for the Hereafter, matching the focus's superior valuation.
Calls worldly enjoyment little and the Hereafter better for the mindful.
Warns against treating the fleeting goods of worldly life as the decisive gain.
Names worldly life as a source of deception for those who make religion play and amusement.
Describes people deceived by worldly life after treating religion as amusement.
Rebukes taking the fleeting goods of this low world while presuming forgiveness.
Identifies wealth and children as a test, directly qualifying the focus's named adornments.
Challenges contentment with worldly life in preference to the Hereafter.
Wealth and children are not signs of favor but a means of testing and punishment in worldly life.
The example of prior peoples enjoying their worldly share warns against imitating their short-term consumption.
Again warns that wealth and children should not cause admiration, since they can become a trial.
The parable of rain-fed worldly life that becomes stubble closely parallels 18:45–46's transience argument.
Those who seek worldly life and its adornment receive its full but limited return here.
Completes the warning: works aimed only at worldly life are nullified in the Hereafter.
What people possess comes to an end, while what is with God remains and recompenses the steadfast.
Righteous action receives a good life and a reward according to the best of what was done.
Seeking the immediate world is contrasted with its limited, divinely apportioned outcome.
Seeking the Hereafter and striving for it receives acknowledged effort, directly complementing enduring righteous deeds.
The Hereafter is declared greater in degrees and preference than worldly portions.
The earth's adornment will be made a barren, level plain, completing 18:7's test of best deeds.
God does not let the reward of those who do good deeds be lost.
The gardens and lasting reward for believers complete the positive side of 18:46's comparison.
The parable of the two garden owners begins the immediate illustration of wealth's unstable prestige.
The two gardens' abundance establishes the material display later shown to be insecure.
The garden owner boasts of greater wealth and more followers, directly echoing wealth and children as worldly status.
The wealthy owner wrongs himself by assuming the garden will never perish.
His expectation of an even better final return exposes the false security drawn from worldly abundance.
The companion's rebuke corrects the garden owner's self-deception and refusal of the Creator.
Exclusive allegiance to God counters the self-sufficient posture produced by wealth.
The instruction to acknowledge God's will and power directly corrects pride in material possession.
The threatened loss of the garden's water shows how quickly worldly assets can become unrecoverable.
The garden's destruction and its owner's regret make the loss of worldly adornment concrete.
After the loss, wealth and followers fail to provide help or self-rescue.
God's reward is declared better and more enduring than Pharaoh's threatened worldly punishment.
Every soul is tested through both evil and good before returning to God, framing possessions as a test rather than a final good.
Explicitly asks whether provision of wealth and children should be mistaken for a hastening of good.
Records the desire for Qarun's worldly display, which 28:80 then corrects by God's better reward.
Everything perishes except God, grounding the distinction between transient possessions and what abides.
Worldly life is amusement and play, while the true life is the abode of the Hereafter.
Warns against being deceived by worldly life and by the deceiver concerning God.
Denies that abundance of wealth and children is a basis for nearness to God.
Warns all people not to let worldly life deceive them.
Promises the steadfast an immeasurable reward, supporting the focus's hope in lasting recompense.
Calls worldly life only temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the lasting home.
Contrasts seeking the harvest of the Hereafter with seeking only the harvest of this world.
The hypothetical universal provision of silver houses and ornament shows luxury is not the measure of divine worth.
Those deceived by worldly life face the consequence of treating God's signs as mockery.
Worldly life is play and amusement, while faith and mindfulness preserve reward beyond material loss.
Wealth and children must not distract believers from God's remembrance; distraction ends in loss.
Wealth and children are explicitly a test, while the great reward is with God.
Love of the immediate world is set against neglect of the Hereafter.
Completes the contrast by naming the abandonment of the Hereafter.
Condemns loving the immediate world and leaving behind a weighty Day.
The transgressor who prefers worldly life begins the negative side of the final value comparison.
Hell is the destination for the one who preferred worldly life.
Fear of standing before the Lord and restraint from desire begin the positive alternative.
Paradise is the destination for the one who restrains desire, supplying the focus's hoped-for outcome.
Human beings are described as intensely attached to wealth, exposing the disposition corrected by 18:46.
Competition for increase distracts people until death, directly addressing accumulation as worldly fixation.
The eventual questioning about worldly blessings supplies an accountability horizon for worldly possessions.
The wealth-hoarder who counts his possessions illustrates the illusion that accumulation secures permanence.
The weighing of heavy good deeds supplies the final measure that outlasts worldly adornment.
A heavy scale of deeds leads to a satisfying life, making righteous action the decisive enduring capital.
Whatever good believers send ahead for themselves will be found with God, affirming the lasting value of deeds.
Neither wealth nor children avail disbelievers against God, denying their ultimate protective value.
Repeats that wealth and children cannot avail against God, directly limiting the worth of the focus's named adornments.
Love of family, acquired wealth, trade, and dwellings must not outrank God, His messenger, and striving in His way.
The hoarding of gold and silver without spending it in God's way shows wealth failing to become righteous action.
Those content with worldly life and at rest in it are contrasted with the neglected signs of the final return.
Explicitly describes people who prefer worldly life to the Hereafter.
The wavering worshipper who loses both this world and the Hereafter illustrates failed worldly calculation.
Trade and sale must not distract people from God's remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving.
Commands seeking the Hereafter through what God has given while retaining a rightful worldly share.
Knowing only the outward aspect of worldly life is contrasted with heedlessness of the Hereafter.
Worldly increase does not grow with God, while giving for God's face is multiplied.
Neither wealth nor children bring people near to God; faith and righteous deeds bring multiplied reward.
Accumulated worldly goods are set below the enduring mercy of the Lord.
Enjoying good things in worldly life is rebuked when it produces arrogant self-indulgence before the final return.
Trade must be left for God's remembrance, making economic gain subordinate to enduring worship.
